questions.question: What is an Angular directive, and what are its main types?
questions.title: Angular Directive Types
questions.direct_answer: A directive is a class that adds behaviour to elements or changes how a part of a template is rendered. Angular has components with templates, attribute directives that change an existing element, and structural directives that create or remove embedded views.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A component is a directive with its own template.
An attribute directive changes an existing element's behaviour or appearance.
A structural directive controls whether and how template views are created.
Built-in control-flow blocks handle common conditions and loops in modern Angular.
A directive selector decides which template element receives its behaviour.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An Angular directive is a class that attaches reusable behaviour to template elements. Angular groups directives into three broad types. A component is a directive with its own view. An attribute directive works with an existing element or component and changes its behaviour, properties, or presentation. A structural directive works with a template and controls embedded view creation.

For example, a custom `[appHighlight]` attribute directive can set a host element's background while it is active. A structural directive can render a template only when a permission is present. In everyday modern templates, built-in blocks such as `@if` and `@for` cover the common conditional and repeated-view cases even though their syntax is not the old star-prefixed directive syntax.

A directive is matched by the selector in its metadata. Inputs can configure it, and host bindings or host listeners can connect it to the element. Because the behaviour is packaged once, many components can use it without copying event handlers.

Directives should add focused view behaviour, not become hidden general-purpose services. A visual rule that CSS alone can express usually belongs in CSS, while shared data access belongs in a service. A custom structural directive is more complex because it owns view creation; it is justified when a reusable rendering policy is not already handled clearly by Angular's built-in control flow.

sections.title: Element behaviour and embedded view creation
sections.content:
An attribute directive receives the host element that matched its selector. It can expose inputs and map state to host properties, classes, styles, attributes, or events. The host element remains in the view; the directive changes how it behaves. Examples include reusable focus treatment, permission-aware disabling, or a consistent interaction state.

A structural directive operates one level higher. Angular gives it a template and a place to insert views. The directive decides whether to create an embedded copy, how many copies to create, and what context each copy receives. This is why structural behaviour changes the visible shape of the template instead of only changing one element.

Components are also directives, but they own a template. A component selector therefore introduces a new view and component instance. Angular allows one component per element, while multiple attribute directives can contribute behaviour to that element.

Modern `@if`, `@for`, and `@switch` blocks are the clearest choice for ordinary branching and repetition. Older applications commonly use `*ngIf` and `*ngFor`. Understanding structural directives is still useful for libraries and special rendering policies, but a custom directive should solve a repeated view concern rather than replace a small condition that is already readable inline.

sections.title: Directive responsibilities
sections.content:
| Kind | Own template? | Main effect | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Component | Yes | Creates an owned view | `<product-card />` |
| Attribute directive | No | Changes an existing host | `[appHighlight]` |
| Structural directive | Uses a template | Creates or removes views | a permission-rendering directive |
| Built-in block | Block body | Common branch or repetition | `@if` and `@for` |

questions.question: How do `@if`, `@for`, and `@switch` control template rendering in Angular?
questions.title: Angular Template Control Flow
questions.direct_answer: `@if` chooses a branch, `@for` repeats a block for collection items, and `@switch` selects a matching case. These blocks create and remove views, while `track` gives repeated items stable identities so Angular can reuse the correct DOM views when a collection changes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@if` renders one branch according to a condition.
`@else if` and `@else` provide the remaining conditional branches.
`@for` repeats a block and requires a `track` expression.
`@switch` selects a strict-equality case without fall-through.

sections.title: Interview answer
Conditional branches and repeated view identity
sections.content:
Each control-flow block owns a set of possible embedded views. When an `@if` condition changes, Angular removes the previous branch view and creates the next one. Child component state inside the removed branch is destroyed with that view. An alias can store the condition result when the same value is needed several times inside the chosen branch.

`@for` solves a different problem: it must keep multiple views aligned with collection items. The `track` expression is the identity contract. With `track product.id`, moving a product lets Angular move or reuse the product's existing view. Tracking a mutable label or using duplicate IDs breaks that contract. Tracking by object identity can work, but new object instances then look like entirely new items.

`@empty` belongs directly after the loop and appears when there are no items. `@switch` is useful when one status has several named presentations, such as loading, ready, and failed. It does not fall through like some JavaScript switch statements.

These blocks should reveal UI states clearly. If the template contains deeply nested conditions or repeats expensive method calls, derive a simpler value in the class. Control flow is responsible for arranging views; it should not become a hidden business-rule engine.

sections.title: Control-flow view selection
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  State[Template state] --> If[@if selects one branch]
  State --> Switch[@switch selects one case]
  Items[Iterable items] --> For[@for matches each track key]
  For --> Reuse[Existing keyed view reused or moved]
  For --> Create[New key creates a view]
  Items -->|empty| Empty[@empty view]
```

questions.question: How do you create and use a custom attribute directive in Angular?
questions.title: Custom Attribute Directives
questions.direct_answer: Create a class with `@Directive`, give it an attribute selector, and connect directive state to the host element with host bindings or listeners. Import the standalone directive into the component whose template uses it, then place the attribute on an element and bind any directive inputs.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Directive inputs make the behaviour configurable by the template.
The `host` metadata can map state to host properties and host events.
A standalone directive must be imported by the component that uses it.
The directive should enhance the host without owning a separate template.

sections.title: Interview answer
Selector matching, input configuration, and host effects
sections.content:
The selector is the entry point. Angular sees an element with `appHighlight` while compiling a template and attaches an instance of the directive. Unlike a component, the directive does not replace the element or add a child template. It works through the host element that is already present.

Inputs turn one behaviour into a reusable tool. An input aliased to `appHighlight` lets the same attribute select and configure the directive. The `host` object then maps expressions to properties, classes, styles, attributes, and events on that host. These expressions use the directive instance, so a signal such as `active()` can drive the host class.

A focus-highlight directive can set an active state on focus and clear it on blur. A component imports it, adds the attribute to inputs that need the behaviour, and supplies an optional colour. The implementation lives in one place while each use remains visible in its template.

Host behaviour can conflict with behaviour declared by a component or another directive on the same element, so names and responsibilities should stay narrow. Direct DOM manipulation should be avoided when a host binding expresses the same result. Also preserve native semantics: a directive can decorate a button, but it should not turn a `div` into a poor imitation of a button.

sections.title: Attribute directive attachment and host update
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Template[Element with appHighlight] --> Match[Directive selector matches]
  Match --> Instance[Directive instance]
  Binding[Bound input value] --> Instance
  Event[Host focus or blur] --> Instance
  Instance --> Host[Host class or style updated]
```
